title: Ὕαιναι
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 340 (= Perry 243). Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« », ⟨ ⟩ for editorial supplements). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Τὰς ὑαίνας φασὶ παρ’ ἐνιαυτὸν ἀλλάττειν τὴν φύσιν καὶ ποτὲ μὲν ἄρρενας γίνεσθαι, ποτὲ δὲ θηλείας.
sentences.tr: Tas hyainas phasi par’ eniauton allattein tēn physin kai pote men arrenas ginesthai, pote de thēleias.
sentences.l: They say that hyenas change their nature in alternate years and become now males, now females.
sentences.n: παρ’ ἐνιαυτόν is 'year and year about', in alternate years. The belief that the hyena changed sex from one year to the next was widely repeated in antiquity, and as widely denied by those who had looked at the animal. ποτὲ μέν … ποτὲ δέ is the ordinary 'now … now'.

sentences.t: Καὶ δή ποτε ὕαινα ἄρσην ⟨πρὸς⟩ ὕαιναν θήλειαν παρὰ φύσιν διετέθη.
sentences.tr: Kai dē pote hyaina arsēn ⟨pros⟩ hyainan thēleian para physin dietethē.
sentences.l: And indeed once a male hyena was disposed ⟨toward⟩ a female hyena contrary to nature.
sentences.i: And so one day a male hyena had unnatural dealings with a female.
sentences.n: ⟨πρός⟩ is Chambry's own supplement — the angle brackets mark a word he adds to complete the construction, the opposite of the square brackets that mark what he deletes. διατίθεμαι πρός τινα is 'to behave toward someone', and παρὰ φύσιν is the decorous Greek for what the male does to the female.

sentences.t: Ἡ δὲ ὑποτυχοῦσα ἔφη· « Ἀλλ’, ὦ οὗτος, οὕτω ταῦτα πράττε ὡς ἐγγὺς τὰ αὐτὰ πεισόμενος. »
sentences.tr: Hē de hypotychousa ephē· « All’, ō houtos, houtō tauta pratte hōs engys ta auta peisomenos. »
sentences.l: And she, taking-up-the-word, said: « Well, you there, do these things in such a way as one who will soon suffer the same. »
sentences.i: And she took up the word and said: « Well, my man, do what you are doing as one who will soon suffer the same himself. »
sentences.n: ὑποτυχοῦσα is the collection's regular verb for cutting in with an answer, not for physical seizing. ὡς with the future participle gives the frame of mind the action is to be done in: 'on the footing that you will soon suffer the same'. ὦ οὗτος is the blunt Greek hail, 'you there'.

sentences.t: Τοῦτο εἰκότως εἴποι ἄν τις πρὸς τὸν ἤδη ἄρχοντα ὁ μετ’ ἐκεῖνον μέλλων, εἰ πλημμελές τι πάσχοι.
sentences.tr: Touto eikotōs eipoi an tis pros ton ēdē archonta ho met’ ekeinon mellōn, ei plēmmeles ti paschoi.
sentences.l: This someone might fittingly say to the man already in office — the one who is to hold it after him — if he should suffer anything improper.
sentences.i: The man next in line for office might fittingly say this to the man who holds it now, if he suffers some wrong at his hands.
sentences.n: A closing formula not among the usual ones: Τοῦτο εἰκότως εἴποι ἄν τις πρός …, 'this someone might fittingly say to …' — compare Τούτῳ τῷ λόγῳ χρήσαιτο ἄν τις πρός …, and the potential optative of the same shape at fable 290. ὁ μετ’ ἐκεῖνον μέλλων stands in apposition to τις and names who the 'someone' is; the verb of ruling is left out and understood from ἄρχοντα. πλημμελές is what is out of tune, and so an offence.
